question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, side a (opposite A) = 5 cm, and side b (opposite B) = 7 cm. Use the sine formula to find all possible values of angle B, correct to 3 significant figures. Explain why there are two possible values.
referenceAnswer: Using the sine formula: $\frac{7}{\sin B} = \frac{5}{\sin 40^\circ}$, so $\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{5} \approx 0.900$. Then $B \approx 64.1^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 64.1^\circ = 116^\circ$. There are two possible values because $\sin \theta = \sin(180^\circ - \theta)$, and both angles give valid triangles when $a < b$ and $a > b \sin A$ — this is the 'ambiguous case' (Case 3).
evidence: In Supplementary Example 4(a): '$\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{5}$, $B = 64.145^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 64.145^\circ$, $\therefore B = 64.1^\circ$ or $116^\circ$' — described as 'An example of Case 3'.

question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, side a = 10 cm, and side b = 7 cm. Find angle B, correct to 3 significant figures. Explain why only one triangle can be formed in this case.
referenceAnswer: Using the sine formula: $\frac{7}{\sin B} = \frac{10}{\sin 40^\circ}$, so $\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{10} \approx 0.450$, giving $B \approx 26.7^\circ$. Only one triangle exists because $a > b$, so side a is longest among the two given sides, making angle A the largest possible angle — thus B must be acute and unique (Case 4).
evidence: Supplementary Example 4(b) computes $\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{10}$ and gives $B = 26.7^\circ$, labelled 'An example of Case 4'.

question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 120°, side a = 15 cm, and side b = 9 cm. Solve the triangle completely: find angles B and C, and side c, all correct to 3 significant figures.
referenceAnswer: By sine formula: $\frac{9}{\sin B} = \frac{15}{\sin 120^\circ}$ → $\sin B = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{15} \approx 0.520$, so $B \approx 31.3^\circ$. Then $C = 180^\circ - 120^\circ - 31.3^\circ = 28.7^\circ$. Finally, $\frac{c}{\sin 28.7^\circ} = \frac{15}{\sin 120^\circ}$ → $c \approx 8.32$ cm.
evidence: Supplementary Example 5(a) shows: '$\sin B = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{15}$, $B = 31.3^\circ$', then finds $C = 28.7^\circ$ and $c = 8.32$ cm — described as 'Case 6'.

question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 120°, side a = $5\sqrt{3}$ cm, and side b = 9 cm. Explain why no triangle can be formed with these measurements.
referenceAnswer: Using the sine formula: $\sin B = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{5\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.900$, so $B \approx 64.2^\circ$. But then $A + B \approx 120^\circ + 64.2^\circ = 184.2^\circ > 180^\circ$, violating the angle sum of a triangle. Hence, no triangle exists (Case 5).
evidence: Supplementary Example 5(b): '$\sin B = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{5\sqrt{3}}$, $B = 64.158^\circ$, $A + B = 184.158^\circ > 180^\circ$, i.e. triangle cannot be formed. ∴ No solution.' — labelled 'Case 5'.

question: In triangle ABC, angle B = 30° and side AB = 20 cm. Kelvin says the shortest possible length of side AC is 10 cm. Verify his claim using trigonometry and explain the geometric condition that gives this minimum.
referenceAnswer: Yes, the claim is correct. The shortest AC occurs when AC is perpendicular to BC (i.e., when triangle ABC is right-angled at C). Then $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{AC}{20}$, so $AC = 20 \sin 30^\circ = 10$ cm. This is the perpendicular distance from A to line BC — the shortest possible distance from A to any point on BC.
